title: How Zalando Built an In-Process Client-Side Load Balancer for One Million Requests per Second
gist: Zalando moved routing for high fan-out internal traffic out of its shared Skipper edge proxy and into the calling process, cutting the Skipper fleet from 50+ pods to 8 and daily deployment cost from $450 to $110 while making latency attribution possible. The team reimplemented Skipper's exact consistent-hash algorithm (xxHash64, 100 virtual nodes) to avoid cache splits during migration, and its own senior engineer concludes almost no one else should copy the approach.

themes.theme: Why routing moved into the process

insights.claim: Zalando's Product Read API batch endpoint fans a single request into up to 100 parallel calls to individual product pods, each hop transiting the shared Skipper edge load balancer, so a batch's latency is set by the slowest of 100 hops through infrastructure the product team did not own.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: High fan-out request patterns multiply any shared-proxy tail latency by the fan-out factor — a structural argument for owning the routing path in read-heavy, latency-SLA services.
insights.quote: As a batch waited on the slowest of 100 hops through infrastructure the team didn't own, they could not separate Skipper latency spikes from their own.
insights.locator: Zalando's Product Read API is designed to serve millions

insights.claim: Zalando's stated design rule is that routing decisions for high fan-out internal traffic belong inside the calling process while edge and single-GET traffic stays on the shared proxy — an explicit split rather than a proxy replacement.
insights.speaker: Conor Gallagher
insights.so_what: A reusable partition for platform teams: keep the managed proxy at the edge, graduate only the fan-out hot path to in-process routing, so the migration is additive rather than a rip-and-replace.
insights.quote: We decided that for high fan-out internal traffic, the routing decision should live inside the calling process itself. Edge traffic, where Skipper excels, should stay exactly where it is.
insights.locator: Conor Gallagher, senior principal engineer at Zalando, explains

insights.claim: The inability to attribute latency spikes between a shared edge proxy and the calling service — not raw throughput — was the trigger for Zalando to build its own load balancer.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Observability boundaries, not performance ceilings, are increasingly what forces infrastructure ownership decisions inside large engineering orgs.
insights.locator: The engineering team at Zalando recently described

insights.claim: Zalando reimplemented Skipper's exact consistent-hash algorithm — xxHash64 with 100 virtual nodes per endpoint — so both the old proxy path and the new in-process path route identical keys to identical pods during migration, with unit tests pinning that behaviour.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Bit-identical hashing between old and new routing paths is the mechanism that lets a cache-dependent service migrate incrementally rather than in a big-bang cutover.
insights.quote: And because both Skipper and our library use the same hash function and the same number of virtual nodes, they produce identical rings for the same set of pods.
insights.locator: The team reimplemented Skipper's exact algorithm

insights.claim: Consistent hashing limits the blast radius of endpoint churn: adding or removing an endpoint remaps only about 1/N of keys, which is what keeps pod-local caches warm as the fleet scales.
insights.speaker: Conor Gallagher
insights.so_what: Cache-churn math is the deciding constraint for any autoscaled, cache-backed service — it determines whether scaling out helps or hurts under load.
insights.quote: This means that adding or removing an endpoint remaps only about 1/N of keys, minimising cache churn.

insights.claim: Zalando replaced control-plane-crashing polling with a watch-based Kubernetes informer and rebuilt a multi-hour deployment pipeline into fast, reversible deploys before ramping the new balancer from 1% to 100% behind feature toggles.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Reversible deploys and percentage ramps are the prerequisite that makes replacing a load-balancing layer survivable at all; teams without them cannot attempt this migration.

insights.claim: To eliminate scale-up latency spikes, Zalando added an N-ring fade-in over 30 seconds on a ^2.5 curve so newly added pods warm only the products they will actually serve.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Gradual traffic ramp shaped by a convex curve is a concrete, copyable pattern for any cache-backed service whose new instances start cold.

insights.claim: Moving the internal fan-out path off the shared proxy shrank Zalando's Skipper fleet from more than 50 pods to 8 and cut deployment daily cost from $450 to $110.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A ~76% daily cost reduction on one path quantifies how much of a shared proxy fleet exists purely to absorb internal east-west fan-out traffic.

insights.claim: The Product Read API serves 25 markets for one of Europe's largest online fashion retailers at around one million requests per second with single-digit-millisecond latency targets, which is the scale that justified custom routing.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Sets the volume threshold at which in-process load balancing pays back — below roughly this scale the engineering cost dominates the savings.
insights.locator: Zalando's Product Read API is designed to serve millions

insights.claim: Zalando's attempt at availability-zone-aware routing, intended to cut inter-AZ network costs, fragmented its caches and triggered DynamoDB read explosions.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: AZ-affinity routing is a common cloud cost optimisation that can silently shift spend into the database tier — a cautionary datapoint for anyone modelling inter-AZ savings.
insights.quote: While Zalando’s attempt at AZ-aware routing was meant to cut inter-AZ costs, it fragmented caches and triggered DynamoDB read explosions.
insights.locator: While Zalando's attempt at AZ-aware routing

insights.claim: Zalando hardened the in-process routing path with a single jittered retry, FIFO overload shedding, and richer logging that exposed brief node-level freezes the balancer now routes around automatically.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Client-side routing surfaces node-level pathologies that a shared proxy hides, converting an unexplained tail into an automatically mitigated one.
insights.locator: With the new approach, they hardened the path

insights.claim: The Zalando engineer who led the work explicitly advises almost everyone not to build their own client-side load balancer, arguing a mature proxy such as Skipper or Envoy already ships consistent-hash routing hardened by thousands of users.
insights.speaker: Conor Gallagher
insights.so_what: The authoring team disclaiming general applicability is the strongest signal that this is an extreme-edge-case pattern, not an emerging default — discount vendor pitches that generalise it.
insights.quote: Should you build your own? For almost everyone, the answer is don't.
insights.locator: Highlighting that Zalando built its own client-side load balancer

insights.claim: Amazon CTO Werner Vogels publicly praised the engineering while saying he dislikes client-side load balancing for a range of reasons, showing the pattern remains contested among senior cloud architects.
insights.speaker: Werner Vogels
insights.so_what: Divergence between hyperscaler leadership and practitioner enthusiasm means client-side LB will stay a niche pattern rather than becoming a managed-service product line.
insights.quote: I am not a big fan of doing this client-side, for a whole slew of reasons, but this is impressive engineering by the Zalando team.
insights.locator: Werner Vogels, CTO of Amazon, writes

insights.claim: An AWS principal engineer says client-side load balancing was a revelation when he moved from Amazon to Google and argues the approach deserves more prominence, indicating the practice is far more normalised inside Google than inside AWS.
insights.speaker: Alexey Kuznetsov
insights.so_what: Divergent internal norms at the two largest cloud providers hint at where managed client-side routing primitives might appear first.
insights.quote: Client side load balancing was kind of a revelation for me when I moved from Amazon to Google.
insights.locator: Alexey Kuznetsov, principal engineer at AWS, comments

insights.claim: A Hacker News commenter argued Zalando should have contributed improvements upstream instead of treating Skipper as a third-party dependency, since Skipper is built and operated by Zalando's own colleagues.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Internal platform teams being treated as external vendors by their own product teams is a recurring organisational failure mode that shows up as duplicated infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: it felt weird that they treated Skipper as a third-party dependency, even though it is developed and operated by their colleagues.
insights.locator: On Hacker News, a user questions the choice

insights.claim: Skipper remains open source on GitHub but Zalando's new client-side load balancer is unpublished and internal only, so the pattern cannot be adopted directly by outsiders.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: No reusable artifact means the ecosystem gets the design lessons but not the code — the competitive advantage stays with Zalando.
insights.locator: While Skipper is open source and available on GitHub
